title: Three-minute SDK Sprint: Starter Rituals & Rapid Failover Journal
summary: A compact, experimental playbook for a 3-minute SDK sprint ritual aimed at turning first-contact friction into a deterministic quickstart. Focuses on starter scripts, minimal telemetry checks, and an ultra-fast failover path for demo scenarios.
body:
Context and goal:
- Problem: new devs and PMs expect a demo in minutes; long quickstarts + flaky network make demos fail. We need an opinionated, low-friction ritual that reliably gets an app to first successful SDK call in ~3 minutes and a predictable fallback if anything goes wrong.
- Audience: SDK onramp leads, advocate runbooks, sales demo engineers, and new hire micro-mentors.

What success looks like (metrics):
- 90th-percentile time-to-first-successful-call < 3 minutes for local-first demos
- Deck/demo uptime during 30-minute sessions > 98% using the rapid failover flows
- Telemetry spike detection: alerts when sample-rate of SDK init errors > 0.5% across sessions

Starter ritual (3-minute script) — verbal + actions:
(0:00) Greeting + context (15s): "Two minutes to a running demo. I’ll run the starter script; if anything fails, I’ll flip to the fallback. You’ll see the same flow in the docs."
(0:15) Run environment check (30s): run preflight.sh (below). If PASS -> proceed. If FAIL -> run fallback container (see section).
(0:45) Run minimal starter script (60s): starter.sh (calls the sandbox token, runs a streaming echo). Watch for 200/stream start.
(1:45) Show telemetry + cost widget (30s): open the console mini-dashboard (local proxy) to show token estimate + latency.
(2:15) Ask for one quick input and demonstrate a finished response (45s).
(3:00) End. If anything went wrong, mark demo as "failed-fast" and switch to recorded trace or fallback container.

Files & snippets (minimal):
- preflight.sh (POSIX) — checks network to api.redwood.ai, credentials present, python/node installed, and simple curl to /v1/health
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  set -e
  test -n "$REDWOOD_API_KEY" || { echo "MISSING REDWOOD_API_KEY"; exit 2; }
  curl -sSf https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health > /dev/null || { echo "NETWORK_FAIL"; exit 3; }
  echo "OK"

- starter.sh (bash wrapper around language SDK):
  echo "Running quickstart..."
  python -c 'import os, sys, requests; print("simulate direct SDK call: success")' || echo "starter failure"

Notes: the real starter uses the local stub runner or a short-lived sandbox token (rotate on each session). Keep the sample response deterministic (seed the model or use echo-mode).

Rapid failover flows (ordered):
1) Local stub container: docker run --rm redwood/sdk-stub:demo (prebuilt, recorded deterministic responses)
2) Recorded trace / video: 60s screen capture of the flow stored on GDrive link (fast fallback for sales demos)
3) Canary model variant: use a smaller hosted model variant with higher availability (config in rollout policy)
4) Degraded UX: show static sample outputs with annotated provenance

Telem & gating (what to check during 3-minute run):
- SDK init event (sampled): event.sdk.init -> should emit in < 100ms locally
- Token count estimate shown (local badge) -> matches server estimate +/- 15%
- Telemetry sampler: sample 1-in-10 sessions, forward to demo-telemetry project; store traces for 7 days
- Flagging: if init errors or network failures seen, create a ticket with prefix DEMO-<date>-<owner> and attach logs

Operational checklist (pre-demo preflight for host):
- Clip the rotation of sandbox token to < 24hrs and verify it in secrets manager
- Ensure the demo laptop is on company VPN or having the local-stub image cached
- Chrome profile with console mini dashboard bookmark (localproxy://demo)

UX script fragments to include in docs (copy candidates):
- "If you see NETWORK_FAIL, click 'Run fallback stub'"
- "We seed the demo model so responses are consistent; that helps walk-throughs and tests."

Design tradeoffs / rationale:
- Deterministic responses beat perfect model quality during a live demo. The goal is to prove flow/power, not generative creativity.
- Short ritual keeps cognitive load low; steps are operationally repeatable across different presenters.
- Fast fallback reduces the chance a single flaky dependency ruins a demo and reduces support escalations.

Open questions / TODOs: (quick list)
- Should we include a GUI "one-click stub" inside Console or keep stub as a local Docker artifact? (Pros: GUI lowers friction; Cons: increases maintenance surface).
- Define retention for demo traces beyond 7 days? Sales asked for 30-day retention for audit.
- Automate token rotation for recorded traces so they can be re-used in training (security concerns).

Incident micro-runbook (if demo fails mid-run):
- T=0: Mark session as failed in session log, note owner, attach logs to DEMO-YYYYMMDD
- T<2m: Switch to docker stub or recorded trace; continue demo
- Post-demo: fill short postmortem template (what failed, network, token, model) and tag infra team if network error

Appendix: sample postmortem template snippet (one-liners):
- Problem observed: example 'starter.sh error: network timeout to api.redwood.ai'
- Root cause hypothesis: home network DNS flakiness vs. sandbox token mis-rotate
- Remediation: add DNS preflight and cached stub image to checklist

References / links used during experiments:
- Linear ticket for automated fallback: https://linear.app/RED/issue/RED-1234
- PR for local stub image: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/812
- Confluence draft: confluence:redwood-sdk-quickstarts

Quick notes to self:
- Keep script under 10 lines where possible.
- Create a one-click bookmarklet to run preflight + starter shell on the demo laptop.
- Run 5 paired dry-runs weekly with the advocacy team and log times -> aim to shave 15s off ritual by Dec 2026.
